records.p: A historical comparative account distinguishes Ramphotyphlops suluensis by approximately 22 midbody scale rows, contrasted with 20 for R. olivaceus and 18 for Gerrhopilus hedraeus. These reported scalation differences still require voucher-level checking under current taxonomy (Uetz et al., 2026). The Sulu Islands Worm Snake is documented on Basilan within Greater Mindanao. Its other published localities lie in the Sulu Archipelago, and a mainland Mindanao occurrence has not been established (Leviton et al., 2018; Uetz et al., 2026). The working checklist assigns this blind snake to forest habitats. Records of the species from Basilan should be distinguished from those in the Sulu Archipelago, and the broad forest category does not document where it shelters or forages. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Yellow-headed Water Monitor is a strongly built lizard with powerful limbs, claws and a muscular neck. Bright yellow markings on the head and body contrast with dark areas, while enlarged scales around the pineal region and transverse dark bands on the belly provide additional characters (Sanguila et al., 2026; Uetz et al., 2026). Cuming’s Water Monitor is documented from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte and Bohol. Populations from the northern islands have been assigned to V. cumingi samarensis (Koch et al., 2010; Uetz et al., 2026). The species is documented in the Agusan Marsh wetland region of Mindanao (Sanguila et al., 2026). At Hijo Forest in Tagum City, this monitor was the most frequently encountered reptile during the survey, and individuals were often observed basking near forest trails and swampy areas (Gamalo et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

Published taxonomic revision distinguishes this monitor by five to eight transverse rows of yellow ocelli on a dark back, a mostly dark head with yellow markings, and a temporal stripe (Welton et al., 2014). The Samar Water Monitor Lizard has been documented on Samar, Bohol, and Leyte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; The Reptile Database, n.d.). The Samar Water Monitor has been described from lowland and coastal habitats, including forest, riparian zones, mangroves, peat-swamp margins, and modified wetlands such as fish ponds and rice paddies. A 2024 Leyte peatland survey documented individuals near peat-swamp forest but did not measure habitat selection (Decena et al., 2024). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: A pitviper with a green to blue-green or darker grey-green ground colour, sometimes bearing irregular dark blotches or crossbars. A pale stripe or series of light spots may run along the outermost dorsal scale row, and the tail often contrasts in colour with the body. The second upper labial joins the scale bordering the facial pit (WildAlert, n.d.). Mindanao populations were treated cautiously as T. cf. flavomaculatus in Sanguila and colleagues’ regional survey (2016), so colour alone should not settle uncertain identifications. The Philippine Yellow-spotted Pitviper has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017; GIZ, 2013). The Philippine Yellow-spotted Pitviper is broadly associated with forests. Documented prey categories include frogs, lizards and rodents; the species uses branches and other elevated vegetation for at least part of its activity (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

Northeastern Leyte observations describe a turquoise to green body, darker brown tail tips in adults and reddish tail tips in juveniles (Decena et al., 2023). The Philippine Keel-throated Pitviper has records from Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). In northeastern Leyte, the species was recorded in arboreal microhabitats (Decena et al., 2023). In northeastern Leyte this viper was recorded on tree branches and saplings, often approximately 1 m above ground, within riparian or forest habitats (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The Hijo account reports sex- and age-linked variation in this pit viper: juveniles and adult males display yellow-green venters and pale bars, whereas adult females show more complex pale and turquoise patterning. Its only Hijo record in the paper was management-reported rather than a survey capture (Gamalo et al., 2023). The Banded Keel-throated Pitviper is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, Mount Lumot, and Surigao del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023; Tirona et al., 2026). A fully arboreal pit viper in comparative habitat records (Uetz et al., 2026). In the Taguibo Watershed of Butuan City, the species was found in both ground and arboreal microhabitats (Sanguila et al., 2021). The species gives birth to live young (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The Loggerhead Sea Turtle has a large, blunt head, powerful jaws and a reddish-brown, heart-shaped carapace. Its shell bears five pairs of lateral scutes, and the jaws are adapted for crushing hard-shelled prey (NOAA Fisheries, n.d., 2026). The Loggerhead Sea Turtle has been documented in the coastal waters of Surigao del Sur, including Hinatuan Bay, and historically from Basilan and Southern Leyte (Byrne & Hines, 2005; Sagun et al., 2005). Loggerhead Turtles use marine environments and coastal waters, while reproduction requires nesting beaches. The species’ diet includes hard-shelled invertebrates, but the presence of animals offshore does not establish nesting at a particular Greater Mindanao beach (NOAA Fisheries, n.d.). Juveniles and adults consume hard-shelled invertebrates including crabs and mollusks. Nesting females return to sandy beaches and deposit clutches in excavated nests (NOAA Fisheries, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

records.p: The Green Sea Turtle has an oval, smoothly edged carapace, a comparatively small head and a short snout. It has one pair of prefrontal head scales and typically four pairs of lateral carapace scutes. Shell colour varies among individuals (NOAA Fisheries, n.d., 2026). The Green Sea Turtle has been documented on Mindanao, including Mayo Bay and Davao Oriental (Jimenez & Inabiogan, 2019). Many adult green turtles graze on seagrass and marine algae, whereas younger animals can consume more animal material. Females nest on beaches and adults can migrate long distances between feeding and nesting grounds (NOAA Fisheries, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

records.p: The Hawksbill Turtle has a narrow head with a strongly hooked beak, two pairs of prefrontal scales and overlapping carapace scutes. Its serrated shell margin and variable brown-and-amber pattern are especially apparent in younger turtles (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, n.d., 2026). The Hawksbill Sea Turtle has been documented on Mindanao, including Mayo Bay and Davao Oriental (Jimenez & Inabiogan, 2019). Hawksbills feed extensively on marine sponges within coral reef habitats. Females come ashore to nest in sandy areas, often within coastal vegetation (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

records.p: The Olive Ridley Sea Turtle has a broadly rounded, olive-grey carapace and a comparatively small head. The shell typically bears five to nine pairs of lateral scutes, sometimes with different counts on the two sides (NOAA Fisheries, n.d., 2026). The Olive Ridley Sea Turtle has been documented on Mindanao, including Mayo Bay and Davao Oriental (Jimenez & Inabiogan, 2019). Olive Ridley Turtles use marine waters and coastal habitats; breeding females come ashore to nest on beaches. Reported mass-nesting behavior from other parts of the species’ range should not be assumed at Greater Mindanao sites without regional evidence (NOAA Fisheries, n.d.). The species consumes crabs, shrimps, other invertebrates and some fish. In parts of its worldwide range, nesting females gather synchronously in large groups termed arribadas; that nesting mode is not assumed for Greater Mindanao (NOAA Fisheries, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

records.p: Unlike hard-shelled marine turtles, the leatherback has a leathery, scale-free carapace marked by longitudinal ridges. Its dark body often bears pale spots (NOAA Fisheries, n.d.). The leatherback’s upper jaw also bears sharply pointed cusps associated with the capture of gelatinous prey (NOAA Fisheries, 2026). The Leatherback Sea Turtle has records from Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). Leatherback Turtles forage in marine waters, where gelatinous zooplankton such as jellyfish and salps are documented prey. Females nest on sandy beaches, although a regional offshore record cannot be taken as proof of a local nesting site (NOAA Fisheries, n.d.). Leatherbacks pursue gelatinous prey such as jellyfish and salps and can dive deeply during foraging. Females deposit eggs in nests dug on sandy beaches (NOAA Fisheries, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

records.p: The Pond Slider has a smooth, moderately domed shell marked with dark and pale streaks and a striped head and neck. The familiar red-orange patch behind the eye is characteristic of the Red-eared Slider subspecies, T. s. elegans, rather than the entire species. The Yellow-bellied Slider, T. s. scripta, instead has a large yellow blotch behind the eye (U.S. Geological Survey, n.d.). The Pond Slider is recorded on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). Studies summarized by the U.S. Geological Survey describe the Pond Slider as an omnivorous aquatic turtle. Adults generally eat more plant matter than juveniles, and females lay eggs in nests excavated on land. Much of this natural-history evidence comes from populations outside the Philippines (U.S. Geological Survey, 2026).

records.p: The Philippine Box Turtle treatment describes a vertebrally keeled carapace, nearly black adult plastron, and a yellow stripe running from the snout through the upper orbital region (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Philippine Box Turtle has records from Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, Davao del Norte, and Lanao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; The Reptile Database, 2023; Sanguila et al., 2026). A 2026 inventory recorded Philippine Box Turtles in disturbed and cultivated areas adjacent to the freshwater swamp forest of Agusan Marsh (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Philippine Box Turtle was separated taxonomically from the broad Cuora amboinensis complex in a recent treatment. Because historical museum and field records often used C. amboinensis for Philippine animals, these reports need locality and diagnostic-voucher review before assignment to the narrower C. philippinensis concept (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: A very large softshell turtle with a smooth, nearly uniform olive-brown carapace in adults and little or no cervical tuberculation. Juveniles may show dark spots on the carapace and head and a yellowish rim; much of this pattern fades with growth (Naturalis Biodiversity Center, n.d.). The Asian Giant Softshell Turtle has been documented at Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary and the Panabo River system of eastern Mindanao, as well as the coastal waters of Zamboanga del Norte (Diesmos et al., 2008; Sy & Antabo-Nogot, 2021). The Asian Giant Softshell Turtle inhabits rivers, tributaries, lakes and marshes and has also been observed in brackish or coastal waters (The Reptile Database, n.d.; Sy & Antabo-Nogot, 2021). An assessment dated 2018 and published in 2021 reports a decreasing global population trend (Choudhury et al., 2021). Cantor’s Giant Softshell Turtle has appeared under several historic species combinations and spellings in the taxonomic literature (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: The oval soft carapace lacks the firm scutes of hard-shelled turtles. A protruding elongated snout and pale ventral surface are useful characters; juvenile carapaces may show dark spotting (U.S. Geological Survey, n.d.). The Chinese Softshell Turtle is recorded on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The regional checklist associates the Chinese Softshell Turtle with rivers and streams. Its presence in the Philippines may involve introduced or traded animals, so aquatic habitat use cannot by itself establish a native Greater Mindanao population. Pelodiscus sinensis has a complex identification history involving several superficially similar Asian softshells. For Philippine observations, a photograph of a generic softshell turtle is insufficient to establish this species or its native status without checking introduction pathways and diagnostic characters (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

PanTHERIA compiles adult mass 49457.6 g and head–body length 1255.0 mm for the historical species concept (Jones et al., 2009). The Philippine Brown Deer has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Lake Lanao, and Sultan Kudarat. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Mount Pangasugan and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Philippine Brown Deer browses shoots, foliage and fruit and may graze in forest clearings and adjacent grassland. Compiled traits also describe ground foraging and activity mainly at night and twilight (Ali et al., 2021; Wilman et al., 2014). The Mammal Diversity Database records the Mariana Islands as the original type locality, where the deer had been introduced (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The species was originally described as cervus Mariannus (A. G. Desmarest, 1822). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

The Greater Mindanao subspecies S. p. mindanensis is described with a mostly black crest and mane and a whitish crown tuft, differing from the forward-fringed head tuft of the Greater Luzon form (IUCN SSC Wild Pig Specialist Group, n.d.). The Philippine Warty Pig has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Busa Mountain Range, Bega Watershed, Lake Lanao, and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Mount Pangasugan (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Warty Pig inhabits forests and adjoining vegetated habitats, including montane and mossy forest in some areas. It eats fallen fruit, underground plant parts and invertebrates and may become more nocturnal in disturbed landscapes (IUCN SSC Wild Pig Specialist Group, n.d.; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Sus philippensis (Nehring, 1886). Its historical type locality is Luzon, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: A shaggy greyish palm civet with a pale mask across the forehead, a small pale mark under each eye and pale spots beside the nostrils; the muzzle and ears are dark. The long, stocky body bears three rows of dark dorsal markings, while the lower legs and the long tail are dark rather than conspicuously ringed. These WildAlert external characters are useful for an initial palm-civet identification but are not a specimen-based key distinguishing all species in the Paradoxurus complex (WildAlert, n.d.). The Philippine Palm Civet is recorded on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range and Mount Apo (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Palm Civet is associated with forests. The species was originally described as Paradoxurus philippinensis (Jourdan, 1837). Its historical type locality is Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 recognizes P. philippinensis following taxonomic separation from the P. hermaphroditus complex. Older Philippine records under P. hermaphroditus require taxon-concept reconciliation (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A series of black spots covers the greyish or tawny body; a dark stripe runs along the dorsal crest, and the tail carries contrasting pale and black bands. The feet are predominantly black (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). The Malay Civet has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo, and Bega Watershed. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Malay Civet uses forest, cultivated land and other modified terrestrial habitats. It is mainly nocturnal and ground-dwelling, occasionally climbing and sheltering in dense vegetation. The civet mainly moves and searches for food at night. It usually travels on the ground, but can climb trees, and shelters in dense vegetation during daylight (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). EltonTraits estimates a diet of endothermic vertebrates (30%), ectothermic vertebrates (30%), invertebrates (10%), other plant material (10%), fruit (10%), other vertebrates (10%), with ground foraging and nocturnal, crepuscular and diurnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). PanTHERIA compiles litter size 1.9 for comparison (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Viverra Tangalunga (J. E. Gray, 1832). Its historical type locality is West Sumatra (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 44–49 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Small Asian Sheath-tailed Bat has records from Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Zamboanga del Norte and Agusan del Sur. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Siargao, records include Siargao Island Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Small Asian Sheath-tailed Bat roosts in caves, including partly lit cavities, on Siargao and in the Agusan provinces of Mindanao. Compiled traits describe mainly aerial foraging on invertebrates (Nuñeza & Galorio, 2014; Perez & Nuñeza, 2020; Warguez et al., 2013; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Vespertilio (Nycticeus) alecto (Eydoux & P. Gervais, 1836). Its historical type locality is Manila, Luzon, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The pale underbody and extensively whitish wing membranes contrast with dark dorsal fur. Adults have a short muzzle; males possess a throat pouch (National Parks Board, 2019). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 66–71 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Field Museum Mindanao bat guide lists adult forearm length as 66–71 mm for Saccolaimus saccolaimus (Ingle et al., Rapid Color Guide No. 49, v1.2). PanTHERIA compiles adult mass 43.0 g and forearm length 71.2 mm for the historical species concept (Jones et al., 2009). The Bare-rumped Sheath-tailed Bat has been documented on Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). The Bare-rumped Sheath-tailed Bat roosts in hollow trees, rock crevices and buildings. It is a nocturnal aerial insectivore that can produce audible clicks during flight (National Parks Board, 2019; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Taphozous Saccolaimus (Temminck, 1838). Its historical type locality is Java, Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The body is grey-brown to buff above with a paler underside. Light-coloured wings appear whitish in flight, and the chin lacks a throat pouch (National Parks Board, 2019). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 61–65 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Black-bearded Tomb Bat has been documented on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Zamboanga del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Black-bearded Tomb Bat roosts in cave crevices and cavities, sometimes forming maternity groups. Studies in Mindanao have recorded insect remains in its diet; compiled traits describe nocturnal aerial foraging (Warguez et al., 2013; Galorio & Nuñeza, 2014; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Taphozous melanopogon (Temminck, 1841). Its historical type locality is Bantam, West Java, Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: A measured Mt Kitanglad male specimen had a 35 mm forearm (Heaney et al., 2006). The Mindanao bat guide reports an adult forearm measurement of approximately 34 mm (elbow to wrist) (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Philippine Tailless Roundleaf Bat has historical reports from the Mount Kitanglad region of Mindanao. These older reports predate the current separation of Coelops hirsutus from related taxa (Heaney et al., 2006; Mammal Diversity Database, 2026; BatNames, 2026). The Philippine Tailless Roundleaf Bat is associated with forests, rivers, streams, caves and karst landscapes. The species was originally described as Chilophylla hirsuta (G. S. Miller, 1910). Its historical type locality is Alag River, opposite mouth of Egbert River, Mindoro, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The original name Phyllorhina antricola was based on a male bat from an abandoned mine near Paracale, Luzon. Peters (1861) reported an ear about 17 mm long and 15 mm wide, a transverse noseleaf with four cells in his terminology, a conspicuous frontal sac in the male, and a tail about 30 mm long, nearly twice the approximately 16.5-mm tibia length. The original male had a forearm about 39 mm long; the wing membranes attached at the tarsus, the fur had pale bases and cinnamon-brown tips, and the wing membranes were brown. These are measurements and observations of the historical type specimen, not verified identification limits for all Philippine populations. The Mammal Diversity Database now treats H. antricola as distinct from the older H. ater complex, but the reported forearm and pelage characters alone do not exclude other small roundleaf bats. Museum-grade comparison of noseleaf, cranial and dental characters is needed for difficult specimens; a flying bat or isolated forearm measurement is not enough. The Philippine Dusky Roundleaf Bat has been documented on Mindanao, including Cotabato (Hollister, 1913). The Philippine Dusky Roundleaf Bat is broadly associated with forests, caves, and karst areas. The species was originally described as Phyllorhina antricola (W. C. H. Peters, 1861). Its historical type locality is Paracali, Luzon I, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 recognizes this bat separately from the historical Hipposideros ater complex (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 44–50 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Fawn-colored Roundleaf Bat is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Zamboanga del Norte, Agusan del Sur, and Cotabato. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Siargao, records include Siargao Island Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Fawn-colored Roundleaf Bat has been recorded roosting in caves on Siargao and in Agusan del Sur (Nuñeza & Galorio, 2014; Perez & Nuñeza, 2020). Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Rhinolophus cervinus (J. Gould, 1854). Its historical type locality is Cape York and Albany Island, Queensland, Australia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao bat guide reports an adult forearm measurement of approximately 47 mm (elbow to wrist) (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Large Mindanao Roundleaf Bat is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Surigao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Large Mindanao Roundleaf Bat is associated with forests, caves and karst landscapes. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Phyllorhina coronata (W. C. H. Peters, 1871). Its historical type locality is Mainit, Surigao del Norte Province, Mindanao, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The large noseleaf and conspicuous pale shoulder patches contrast with a generally dark upper coat. Colour and measurements vary across the species’ broad regional range (Wilson & Mittermeier, 2019). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 77–89 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Diadem Roundleaf Bat has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Mayo, Mount Kitanglad Range, Lanao del Norte, and Cotabato. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Heaney et al., 2006). The Diadem Roundleaf Bat roosts in caves on Siargao and Mindanao. Dietary records include insect remains, and compiled traits describe nocturnal aerial insect foraging (Nuñeza & Galorio, 2014; Perez & Nuñeza, 2020; Galorio & Nuñeza, 2014; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Rhinolophus diadema (É. Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, 1813). Its historical type locality is "Timor [Island]." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 42–48 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Philippine Forest Roundleaf Bat has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, and Surigao del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013; Heaney et al., 2006). The Philippine Forest Roundleaf Bat is associated with forests and has been documented roosting in caves, mines, culverts, hollow trees and spaces among tree buttresses (Heaney et al., 2006). Day roosts include caves, mines, culverts and tree hollows (Heaney et al., 2006). Compiled traits describe nocturnal aerial foraging on invertebrates (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Phyllorhina obscura (W. C. H. Peters, 1861). Its historical type locality is "Paracali [= Paracali, Camarines Norte Province], Luzon," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The large ears join across the forehead, and the upright noseleaf is conspicuous. This bat lacks the external tail characteristic of many other insectivorous bats (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 57–63 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Lesser Asian False-vampire has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Lesser Asian False-vampire roosts in caves, hollow trees and sometimes buildings. Mindanao observations include roosts in large dao trees. Its food includes insects and small vertebrates (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.; Nuñeza & Galorio, 2014; Gamalo et al., 2023; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Vespertilio Spasma (Linnaeus, 1758). Its historical type locality is Ternate, Molucca Islands, Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: A small bent-winged bat with brown to dark grey dorsal fur, no noseleaf and a forearm approximately 36–40 mm long in the cited treatment. Relative to larger bent-winged bats, small body size is helpful but not a sole diagnostic feature (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 34–39 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Little Long-fingered Bat is recorded on Mindanao, Bohol, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013; Heaney et al., 2006). The Little Long-fingered Bat uses caves, abandoned mines, tunnels and other cavities as day roosts. Its night-time foraging habitats are not necessarily limited to those roost sites. Day roosts have been reported in caves, abandoned mines, tunnels and other cavities. Nursery sites often occur in limestone caves; the cited observations include populations outside the Philippines (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). EltonTraits estimates a diet of invertebrates (100%), with aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). PanTHERIA compiles gestation 132.7 days, litter size 1.0 for comparison (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Miniopteris Australis (Tomes, 1858). Its historical type locality is Lifu Island, Loyalty Islands, New Caledonia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 51–55 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Great Long-fingered Bat is recorded on Mindanao, Bohol, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park, Zamboanga del Norte, and North Cotabato. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Great Long-fingered Bat is associated with forests, caves and karst landscapes. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Vespertilio tristis (G. R. Waterhouse, 1845). Its historical type locality is "Philippine Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Lesser Naked Bat has an adult forearm length of 73–78 mm in the Field Museum guide to the bats of Mindanao (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Lesser Naked Bat is recorded across Mindanao, including Davao del Sur, Misamis Oriental, Sarangani, South Cotabato and Zamboanga del Norte (IUCN, 2019; Ingle et al., n.d.). In the Philippines, the Lesser Naked Bat has been found roosting in hollow trees and coconut palms, as well as occasionally in caves (IUCN, 2019). Compiled ecological traits describe nocturnal aerial foraging on invertebrates (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Cheiromeles parvidens (G. S. Miller & Hollister, 1921). Its historical type locality is "Pinedapa, Middle Celebes [= Sulawesi]," Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 40–43 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Wrinkle-lipped Free-tailed Bat has been reported from Leyte, including Southern Leyte (GIZ, 2013). The Wrinkle-lipped Free-tailed Bat roosts in caves, sometimes in large colonies, and also uses rock crevices and buildings. It hunts flying insects over varied landscapes, including agricultural land (IUCN, 2020; Srilopan et al., 2026). The original master checklist uses Chaerephon plicata. Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 and the IUCN assessment use Mops plicatus (Buchanan, 1800); the older spelling and combination remain traceable through the taxonomic history (IUCN, 2020; Mammal Diversity Database, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 39–45 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Sulawesian Free-tailed Bat has been documented on Mindanao, including Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Sulawesian Free-tailed Bat is associated with forests, rivers and streams, and cultivated areas. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Nyctinomus sarasinorum (A. B. Meyer, 1899). Its historical type locality is "Batulappa, nördlich vom See von Tempe [= north of Lake Tempe], SW Central Celébes [= Sulawesi]," Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A 2025 Luban Island study reassessed a colony initially identified as A. jubatus and described Pteropus alternatives (Ramos & Calica, 2025). Bat Conservation International describes distinctive gold-colored fur on the head of the giant golden-crowned flying fox (Bat Conservation International, n.d.). The giant golden-crowned flying fox is very large, with golden fur on the head contrasting with its darker body; identification depends on visible characters and size context (Bat Conservation International, n.d.). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 165–215 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). PanTHERIA compiles adult mass 1087.0 g and forearm length 188.0 mm for the historical species concept (Jones et al., 2009). The Golden-capped Flying Fox has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Malindang Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Apo, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Golden-capped Flying Fox roosts in trees, sometimes alongside other large flying foxes, and feeds heavily on figs in mature lowland forest. Philippine tracking has also recorded movements across agricultural and built-up areas (Bat Conservation International, n.d.; Constantino et al., 2026; Wilman et al., 2014). The Bat Conservation International account notes forest loss, hunting and roost disturbance as central concerns (Bat Conservation International, n.d.). A 2025 Luban Island study reassessed an earlier golden-crowned flying fox identification as Pteropus spp. (Ramos & Nemenzo-Calica, 2025). The species was originally described as Pteropus jubatus (von Eschscholtz, 1831). Its historical type locality is "Insel [= Island] Luzon, Manilla," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

records.p: The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 45–50 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Mindanao Pygmy Fruit Bat has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kalatungan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Tuminungan, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026; Lama et al., 2024; Heaney et al., 2006). The Mindanao Pygmy Fruit Bat occurs in montane forest, with Mount Kitanglad records particularly numerous in high-elevation mossy forest. Compiled traits describe nocturnal fruit-feeding in trees (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Alionycteris paucidentata (Kock, 1969). Its historical type locality is Mount Kitanglad, Bukidnon Province, Mindanao, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A short tail, large eyes and pale edges to the ears and wing bones characterize this fruit bat. Males commonly show a reddish neck collar, whereas females may have a more yellowish collar (National Parks Board, 2019). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 58–68 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Lesser Short-nosed Fruit Bat is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kalatungan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Yangurin et al., 2025; Heaney et al., 2006). The Lesser Short-nosed Fruit Bat feeds on fruit and nectar and may roost under leaves, in trees or in buildings. Mindanao field studies recorded it at lower-elevation sites and identified fig seeds among sampled food remains (Heaney et al., 2006; National Parks Board, 2019; Galorio & Nuñeza, 2014; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Pachysoma brachyotis (S. Müller, 1838). Its historical type locality is Dewei (= Dewai) River, Borneo (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: A large fruit bat with medium to pale-brown fur and face, and paler brown flight membranes interrupted by conspicuous white blotches, especially along the leading wing edge and near the tip. The IUCN account reports a forearm of 135–145 mm and contrasts it with the nearly black wings and face of the similar-sized Pteropus hypomelanus. The IUCN source spells the specific name leucopterus; this manuscript follows the feminine ending leucoptera used by the Mammal Diversity Database (Waldien & Duya, 2020, summarizing Heaney et al., 2010). Within Greater Mindanao, the White-winged Flying Fox has a documented distribution on Dinagat Island. Published range treatments place the species otherwise in the Luzon faunal region and do not establish a regular population on Mindanao mainland. The regional account follows Dinagat records reported under the spelling Desmalopex leucopterus, while retaining the checklist name Desmalopex leucoptera (Waldien & Duya, 2020; DENR-BMB, 2018). The White-winged Flying Fox is associated with forests. The species was originally described as Pteropus leucopterus (Temminck, 1853). Its historical type locality is "îles Philippines." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 notes the transfer from Pteropus to Desmalopex and the feminine adjectival ending leucoptera rather than historical leucopterus. Older literature under Pteropus must be reconciled before extracting records (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The taxonomic revision treats this as a large Dyacopterus fruit bat: examined specimens had forearms exceeding approximately 90 mm and greatest cranial lengths exceeding approximately 40 mm, with palatal ridge counts also useful in distinguishing congeners. These were characters used in the original comparison, not standalone cutoffs for all populations (Helgen et al., 2007). The Philippine Large-headed Fruit Bat has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Large-headed Fruit Bat is broadly associated with forests. The species was originally described as Dyacopterus rickarti (K. M. Helgen, Kock, Gomez, & Ingle in K. M. Helgen, Kock, Gomez, Ingle, & M. H. Sinaga, 2007). Its historical type locality is "San Isidro (17°27'N, 120°37'E), Luzon (Abra Province), Philippines." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: This comparatively large dawn bat has a long narrow muzzle. The species treatment reports forearm measurements of about 67–82 mm and distinguishes it from related taxa using cranial measurements (Wilson & Mittermeier, 2019). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 67–82 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Philippine Dawn Bat has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Awasian Water Forest Reserve, Mount Magdiwata, Zamboanga del Norte, and Misamis Oriental. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Mount Lobi Range (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Dawn Bat feeds on nectar and can pollinate forest trees, linking its foraging ecology to flowering plants (Roño et al., 2021). Compiled traits describe nectar feeding, arboreal foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Eonycteris robusta (G. S. Miller, 1913). Its historical type locality is "cave at Montalban [Rizal Province], Luzon, Philippine Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

A long, narrow muzzle and protrusible tongue are suited to feeding at flowers. The elongate head differs from the short muzzle of many fruit bats (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 67–80 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Lesser Dawn Bat is recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Sugarloaf, Mount Kampalili, Zamboanga del Norte, and Zamboanga del Sur. On Leyte, records include Mount Lobi Range (GBIF.org, 2026; Yangurin et al., 2025). The Lesser Dawn Bat uses caves as roosts and visits flowers for nectar and pollen. Mindanao observations include bats roosting on partly illuminated cave walls (Warguez et al., 2013). The species was originally described as Macroglossus spelæus (Dobson, 1871). Its historical type locality is "Penang, Moulmein, the Nicobar and Andaman Islands." Restricted by K. Andersen in 1912 to "Farm Caves, Moulmein [= Mwalamyaing, Myanmar]." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 46–53 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Fischer's Pygmy Fruit Bat has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Kalatungan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Heaney et al., 2006). Fischer’s Pygmy Fruit Bat occurs in montane forest on Mount Kitanglad and was less frequently recorded in the highest mossy-forest survey site. Compiled traits describe fruit feeding (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Haplonycteris fischeri (B. Lawrence, 1939). Its historical type locality is "Bignay, Mt. Halcon, Mindoro," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 80–91 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Philippine Harpy Fruit Bat is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Yangurin et al., 2025). The Philippine Harpy Fruit Bat inhabits montane forest and has been observed feeding on Freycinetia flowers and fruits (Heaney et al., 2006; Yangurin et al., 2025). The Mammal Diversity Database records the original specimen from Mindoro at approximately 1,524 m elevation (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The species was originally described as Harpyionycteris Whiteheadi (O. Thomas, 1896). Its historical type locality is "Mindoro [Island], Philippines, alt. 5000 feet [= 1524 m]." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The slender muzzle and long extensible tongue are suited to blossom feeding. Adult males have a pink, V-shaped chest gland (Bat Conservation International, n.d.). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 41–45 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Lesser Long-tongued Blossom Bat has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023; Heaney et al., 2006). The working checklist assigns the Lesser Long-tongued Fruit Bat to caves and karst areas, but its existing natural-history account describes nectar and pollen feeding at flowers. Roosting context and floral foraging habitat should be distinguished rather than equating the cave category with feeding habitat. Feeds chiefly on nectar and pollen at large flowers, with fruit included in some populations. Flower visits documented in regional studies include banana and other large-flowered plants (Bat Conservation International, n.d.). EltonTraits estimates a diet of nectar (80%), fruit (20%), with arboreal foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). PanTHERIA compiles gestation 125.1 days, litter size 1.0 for comparison (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Pteropus minimus (É. Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, 1810). Its historical type locality is Java, Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: Males bear a more developed scented chest ruff than females. The cited mammal treatment reports forearm measurements around 76–91 mm, with a relatively robust build for a small Philippine fruit bat (Wilson & Mittermeier, 2019). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 76–90 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Greater Musky Fruit Bat has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Greater Musky Fruit Bat is associated with forests, caves and karst landscapes. The species was originally described as Pachysoma (Ptenochirus) Jagorii (W. C. H. Peters, 1861). Its historical type locality is Daraga, Albay, Luzon, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A short, sturdy muzzle and dark body distinguish this small fruit bat in field descriptions. Published captures from Calicoan, eastern Samar, describe a forearm of 60–78 mm, shorter on average than the 76–90 mm reported for P. jagorii (Fernandez et al., 2020). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 60–78 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Lesser Musky Fruit Bat has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Heaney et al., 2006). The Lesser Musky Fruit Bat has been recorded in caves in Agusan del Sur, within a landscape subject to human disturbance (Perez & Nuñeza, 2020). Compiled traits describe fruit feeding, arboreal foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Ptenochirus minor (Yoshiyuki, 1979). Its historical type locality is Baracatan, Mount Talomo, Davao City, Mindanao, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: A fruit bat with a dark grey head and muzzle, a conspicuous rusty-brown ruff around the neck and shoulders, and grey-brown to rusty body fur. Relative to typical Ptenochirus, P. wetmorei has an exceptionally reduced tail that may appear externally absent and a weak or inconspicuous groove on the inner face of the upper canine. It was once described under Megaerops because of its reduced tail, but phylogenetic comparisons support its placement in Ptenochirus. Reliable discrimination from similar fruit bats still requires careful dental and cranial comparison (Almeida, Simmons & Giannini, 2020). The Mindanao Fruit Bat has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Magdiwata, Mount Kampalili, Mount Lumot, Mount Daguma, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Yangurin et al., 2025). The Mindanao Fruit Bat is associated with forests. The species was originally described as Megaerops wetmorei (E. H. Taylor, 1934). Its historical type locality is Cotabato near Tatayan, Mindanao Island, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 places wetmorei in Ptenochirus, rather than the historical genus Megaerops, following Almeida and colleagues (2020). Earlier references may use Megaerops wetmorei (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: A comparatively bare upper surface of the lower leg helps distinguish this flying fox from several congeners. The cited species account reports a forearm of about 121–150 mm across its sampled range (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 136–149 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Island Flying Fox is recorded on Mindanao, Dinagat, and Leyte. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Island Flying Fox uses forest and human-modified landscapes, with tracking studies documenting nightly movements away from roosts (Constantino et al., 2026). The species was originally described as Pteropus hypomelanus (Temminck, 1853). Its historical type locality is "L'île de Ternate [= Ternate Island]," Moluccas, Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: An attributed mammal account describes a small flying fox with mostly brown, sometimes grey fur and adult mass of about 145–200 g (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 94–113 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Field Museum Mindanao bat guide lists adult forearm length as 94–113 mm for Pteropus pumilus (Ingle et al., Rapid Color Guide No. 49, v1.2). PanTHERIA compiles adult mass 184.1 g and forearm length 108.0 mm for the historical species concept (Jones et al., 2009). The Little Golden-mantled Flying Fox has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). The Little Golden-mantled Flying Fox inhabits tropical lowland forest, where it feeds on plant material and may gather in small roosting groups (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). The species was originally described as Pteropus pumilus (G. S. Miller, 1910). Its historical type locality is "Palmas Island [= Miangas Island], southeast of Mindanao," Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 118–133 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Philippine Gray Flying Fox has been documented on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Gray Flying Fox is associated with forests and cultivated areas. Its cited trait compilation characterizes it as a fruit-eating, nocturnal, arboreal forager, but does not provide a region-specific comparison of forest and agricultural habitat use (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled traits describe fruit feeding, arboreal foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Pteropus speciosus (Andersen, 1908). Its historical type locality is "Malanipa Island, off [west coast of] Zamboanga," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

A very large flying fox with a fox-like head and pointed ears. Reported adult forearm length is approximately 180–220 mm, with body mass generally 0.6–1.1 kg (Norton, 2011). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 179–204 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Large Flying Fox has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Mount Lobi Range and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Large Flying Fox roosts in trees, including mangroves and forest groves, and feeds on fruit, flowers and nectar. Philippine observations include roosts in forest patches adjoining agricultural and grassland areas (Norton, 2011; Heaney et al., 2006; Stier & Mildenstein, 2005). The species was originally described as Vespertilio Vampyrus (Linnaeus, 1758). Its historical type locality is "Asia." Restricted by K. Andersen in 1912 to "Java," Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

Kitanglad, 19 captured bats at 1,600 m were assigned to the smaller form and one at 1,450 m to the larger form (Heaney et al., 2006). The Arcuate Horseshoe Bat has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Sugarloaf, Mount Magdiwata, Zamboanga del Norte, and Zamboanga del Sur. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Arcuate Horseshoe Bat roosts in caves, including caves on Siargao, and forages on insects at night (Nuñeza & Galorio, 2014; Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Rhinolophus arcuatus (W. C. H. Peters, 1871). Its historical type locality is "Luzon," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The species also uses warm, humid cave or mine roosts, often in small numbers (Australian Museum, 2024). EltonTraits estimates a diet of invertebrates (100%), with aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Rhinolophus Philippinensis (G. R. Waterhouse, 1843). Its historical type locality is Luzon, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

Its historical type locality is "Manila," Luzon, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Field Museum’s Mindanao bat guide listed the Javan Pipistrelle as Pipistrellus javanicus and gave an adult forearm range of 32–36 mm. The current genus is Alionoctula. This is a small vespertilionid bat for which identification should combine forearm measurements with dental and cranial characters from a bat key; the published forearm range alone overlaps with that of the Least Pipistrelle at approximately 32 mm. Recent work also highlights cryptic members of the javanicus species group, so an isolated size measurement is not a secure voucher identification (Ingle, Sedlock, & Heaney, n.d.; American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The Javan Pipistrelle is recorded from Mindanao, including the Mount Balatukan Range of Misamis Oriental and the Bukidnon region (Wilson & Mittermeier, 2019; Ingle et al., n.d.; ASM, 2026). The Javan Pipistrelle is a nocturnal insectivore that roosts in tree ferns, fallen logs, caves and buildings. A Mindanao roost in Bukidnon was documented alongside horseshoe and leaf-nosed bats (Wilson & Mittermeier, 2019). The species was originally described as Scotophilus Javanicus (J. E. Gray, 1838). Its historical type locality is Java, Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 places this bat in Alionoctula, following the 2025 reassessment by Zhukova and colleagues; older sources used Pipistrellus (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Narrow-winged Pipistrelle was described under the name Pipistrellus stenopterus in a Southeast Asian comparative account. Its short fur is dark chocolate to reddish brown, with blackish ears and wing membranes, a heavy muzzle and rounded ears bearing a broad, forward-angled tragus. The fifth metacarpal is shorter than the fourth, producing characteristically narrow wings. The cited study reports adult forearm lengths of 37–42 mm (Leong et al., 2010). The Narrow-winged Pipistrelle has been recorded on Mindanao (Ingle et al., n.d.; ASM, 2026). The Narrow-winged Pipistrelle is broadly associated with forests and habitats along rivers and streams. The species was originally described as Vesperugo stenopterus (Dobson, 1875). Its historical type locality is "Sarawak, Borneo," Malaysia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 records a transfer from Pipistrellus to Alionoctula following Zhukova and colleagues (2025). Earlier regional literature may therefore be indexed under the former genus (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

In the Field Museum guide to Mindanao bats, the Least Pipistrelle appears under the earlier name Pipistrellus tenuis, with an adult forearm range of 30–32 mm. It is currently placed in Alionoctula. Although generally smaller than the Javan Pipistrelle in that guide, the reported ranges meet at 32 mm, so forearm length is only a preliminary sorting character. Dental, skull and other diagnostic measurements should be checked before reporting a definitive identification, especially because older tenuis records may refer to differing taxonomic concepts (Ingle, Sedlock, & Heaney, n.d.; American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The Least Pipistrelle is documented from Mindanao (Ingle et al., n.d.; ASM, 2026). The Least Pipistrelle is associated with forests and waterways. The species was originally described as Vespertilio tenuis (Temminck, 1840). Its historical type locality is Sumatra, Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 notes both the transfer from Pipistrellus to Alionoctula and a historical species delimitation that included A. murrayi. Older name-based records require specimen or taxonomic-concept confirmation before transfer (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Peters’s Pipistrelle has dark chocolate-brown, long woolly dorsal fur with paler tips that produce a frosted appearance. A recently examined specimen also showed broad rounded ears, a short blunt tragus, a small patch of pale fur near the hindlimb and anus, and a slightly projecting tail tip. Identification among similar pipistrelles may require dental or genetic comparison (Guo et al., 2026). The Peters's Pipistrelle has been documented on Mindanao, including Pasonanca area (GBIF.org, 2026). The Peters's Pipistrelle is associated with forests, settlements, and other disturbed areas. The species was originally described as Vesperugo petersi (A. B. Meyer, 1899). Its historical type locality is Minahassa, northern Sulawesi, Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 33–35 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Hardwicke's Woolly Bat has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Lumot, and Misamis Oriental. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Hardwicke's Woolly Bat is associated with forests. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). A comparative mammal-trait compilation lists a litter size of approximately one young for this bat (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Vespertilio hardwickii (Horsfield, 1824). Its historical type locality is Java, Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide reports an adult forearm measurement of approximately 35 mm (elbow to wrist) (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Clear-winged Woolly Bat has records from Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range and Mount Hilong-Hilong (GBIF.org, 2026). The Clear-winged Woolly Bat is associated with forests and shrublands. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Vespertilio pellucidus (G. R. Waterhouse, 1845). Its historical type locality is Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 30–31 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Whitehead's Woolly Bat has records from Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range (GBIF.org, 2026). The Whitehead's Woolly Bat is associated with forests, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open areas, and cultivated areas. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Kerivoula Whiteheadi (O. Thomas, 1894). Its historical type locality is "Isabella, N.E. Luzon," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

In the 2025 taxonomic revision, the Philippine type series is unusually small within the Murina cyclotis group. The authors reported forearm lengths of 33.7 mm for the measured male and 35.8 mm for the measured female; the dorsal fur shows greyish-buff bases with reddish-brown tips. Measurements refer to these specimens, not a known species-wide range (Eger et al., 2025). The Alvarez's Tube-nosed Bat has records from Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Alvarez's Tube-nosed Bat is associated with forests, caves and karst landscapes. The taxonomic series includes postlactating females recorded in May on Mt. Hamiguitan and in August on Cebu. These are dated reproductive-condition observations and do not establish a fixed breeding season across the species (Eger et al., 2025). The species was originally described as Murina alvarezi (Eger, Sedlock, B. K. Lim, & Heaney, 2025). Its historical type locality is Cebu Province, Cebu Island (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: Tubular nostrils project from the nose, and the ears are short and rounded with tapered, triangular tragi. Both reddish-brown and greyer pelage forms are described (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 36–39 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Field Museum Mindanao bat guide lists adult forearm length as 36–39 mm for Murina cyclotis (Ingle et al., Rapid Color Guide No. 49, v1.2). PanTHERIA compiles adult mass 9.3 g and forearm length 34.4 mm for the historical species concept (Jones et al., 2009). The Round-eared Tube-nosed Bat has records from Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Magdiwata, Agusan del Norte, and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The Round-eared Tube-nosed Bat is associated with forests. The cited account describes maneuverable, low-level flight and roosting in sheltered foliage. Some observations come from mainland Southeast Asia rather than the Philippines (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). PanTHERIA compiles litter size 2.0 for comparison (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Murina cyclotis (Dobson, 1872). Its historical type locality is Darjeeling, India (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: Described as the largest Murina in the 2025 Philippine revision. The back has three-coloured hairs with pale-grey bases, buff middle portions and reddish-brown tips, contrasting with a predominantly white throat and central belly. The proximal half of the tail membrane carries long pale-orange hairs, and long hairs cover the feet beyond the claws; the ear has a notch along its rear edge. Its teeth resemble those of M. cyclotis, but it is larger in body and skull dimensions, and genetic and cranial features support separation. Field appearance alone is not conclusive for an uncatalogued tube-nosed bat (Eger et al., 2025). The Hilong-hilong Tube-nosed Bat has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hilong-Hilong and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Hilong-hilong Tube-nosed Bat is broadly associated with forests. The species was originally described as Murina hilonghilong (Eger, Sedlock, B. K. Lim, & Heaney, 2025). Its historical type locality is Mount Hilong-Hilong Range, Surigao del Sur, Mindanao, at approximately 85 m elevation (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Described in 2025, Murina hilonghilong is based on specimens from the Mount Hilong-Hilong Range in Surigao del Sur, including holotype FMNH 190118 from approximately 85 m elevation (Eger et al., 2025).

records.p: The 2025 diagnosis reports a forearm length of 30.8–33.4 mm in its examined specimens, tricolored dorsal fur with darker bases and lighter intermediate bands, and reduced hair coverage of the wing membranes compared with some related Philippine tube-nosed bats. The published measurements are sample-bounded, not universal identification limits (Eger et al., 2025). The Philippine Tube-nosed Bat has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kampalili, and Davao Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Tube-nosed Bat is associated with forests. The species was originally described as Murina philippinensis (Eger, Sedlock, B. K. Lim, & Heaney, 2025). Its historical type locality is Cebu Province, Cebu Island (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The 2025 revision of Philippine Murina recognized M. philippinensis as separate from populations previously placed within the M. suilla complex (Eger et al., 2025).

Waterhouse, 1845). Its historical type locality is "Philippine Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

Gray, 1847). Its historical type locality is Nepal (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Apo Natural Park, and Misamis Oriental. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Rohu's Bat is associated with montane environments. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 47–53 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Lesser Asian Yellow Bat has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Mayo, North Cotabato, and Bukidnon. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Lesser Asian Yellow Bat occupies settlements and cultivated environments, roosting in buildings, palm fronds and tree hollows (Wilman et al., 2014). Documented shelters include buildings, palm fronds and tree hollows. This insectivorous bat can be encountered near settlements, particularly where insects gather around lights (IUCN, 2019). EltonTraits estimates a diet of invertebrates (100%), with aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). PanTHERIA compiles gestation 110.0 days, litter size 1.5 for comparison (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Scotophilus Kuhlii (Leach, 1821). Its historical type locality is India (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The gliding membrane connects the forelimbs and hindlimbs and extends around the digits, distinguishing the colugo from arboreal mammals without a patagium (Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Colugo is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Dinagat, and Leyte, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Philippine Colugo forages among forest trees and has been recorded during surveys of Hijo Forest in Mindanao (Wischusen & Richmond, 1998; Gamalo et al., 2023). The species was originally described as Lemur volans (Linnaeus, 1758). Its historical type locality is "Asia." Restricted by O. Thomas in 1908 to the "Philippine Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The original species description highlighted its distinctive stiff, golden-toned dorsal hairs, although the density and apparent color of these hairs varies among individuals (Heaney & Morgan, 1982). The Dinagat Gymnure has been documented on Dinagat (GBIF.org, 2026; Heaney & Morgan, 1982). The Dinagat Gymnure is associated with forests. Compiled dietary traits include invertebrates and endothermic vertebrates, with ground foraging and nocturnal and crepuscular activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Podogymnura aureospinula (Heaney & G. S. Morgan, 1982). Its historical type locality is "Plaridel, Albor Municipality, Dinagat Island, Surigao del Norte Province, Republic of the Philippines." Interpreted by D. R. Frost and colleagues in 1991 as "10°12'N, 125°35'E." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: The 2023 description notes golden-yellow streaks formed by specialized guard hairs. In the examined regional series, mean head-and-body length was approximately 171 mm for Mt. Hamiguitan specimens and 145 mm for Mt. Kampalili specimens (Balete et al., 2023). The Eastern Mindanao Gymnure has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kampalili, and Davao Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Eastern Mindanao Gymnure inhabits ultramafic, montane and mossy forests in eastern Mindanao (Balete et al., 2023). The species was originally described as Podogymnura intermedia (Balete, Heaney, Rickart, Quidlat, Rowsey, & L. E. Olson, 2023). Its historical type locality is "3.7 km S, 1.4 km E of Mt. Hamiguitan peak, Mati Municipality, Davao Oriental Province, Mindanao Island, Philippines, 950 m elev., 6° 42’ 26.2” N, 126° 11’ 42.8” E." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The smallest recognized Podogymnura in the 2023 revision, with head-and-body length 137–152 mm, a short tail of 49–66 mm, and long, soft dark reddish-brown dorsal fur bearing fine golden-brown tips. Ears and feet are pale; the tail is grey-brown above and almost unpigmented below. It differs clearly in its soft coat and smaller size from the larger, bristly P. aureospinula; it also has subtler golden spotting than P. intermedia. External measurements overlap slightly with P. truei, so specimen-based cranial comparisons may be required (Balete et al., 2023). The Kitanglad Gymnure has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kalatungan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Kitanglad Gymnure is broadly associated with forests. The species was originally described as Podogymnura truei minima (Sanborn, 1953). Its historical type locality is Mt. Kitanglad, Bukidnon Province, Mindanao Island, Philippines, 1600 m (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 separates P. minima from P. truei based on the 2023 taxonomic reassessment by Balete and colleagues. Historical P. truei records may mix these taxa (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A Field Museum Mindanao rapid color guide reports head-and-body length of 130–152 mm, tail length of 45–65 mm and hind-foot length of 31–37 mm. These are comparative field-guide measurements, not a complete diagnosis (Heaney et al., n.d.). The Mount Apo Gymnure has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Apo, Mount McKinley, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). Compiled dietary traits include invertebrates and endothermic vertebrates, with ground foraging and nocturnal and crepuscular activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The Mount Apo Gymnure is associated with forests. Arthropods occurred in all 31 examined stomachs; earthworms in 55% (Heaney et al., 2006). The species was originally described as Podogymnura truei (Mearns, 1905). Its historical type locality is "Mount Apo at 6,000 feet [= 1829 m] altitude, southern Mindanao, Philippine Islands." Interpreted by D. R. Frost and colleagues in 1991 as "6°59'N, 125°16'E." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The 2023 revision of Podogymnura recognizes P. minima as distinct from populations formerly assigned to P. truei (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A small, dark-furred white-toothed shrew. Miller’s original 1910 account described the taxon as Crocidura beatus and compared its color and skull with C. grayi and C. halconus; the Mount Bliss holotype was darker across nearly the whole back and had a slightly less robust skull. That single adult male measured 77 mm head-and-body length, 55 mm tail length and 19.2 mm skull condylobasal length. These figures describe the holotype, not the size variation of the species. Because the skull difference requires direct comparison, external color alone is insufficient to confirm a questionable specimen (Miller, 1910). The Mindanao White-toothed Shrew has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kalatungan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Pasonanca area, Mount Matutum, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Mount Pangasugan (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mindanao White-toothed Shrew occurs in montane and mossy forest on Mount Kitanglad (Heaney et al., 2006). In three stomachs examined from Mt. Kitanglad (reported as Crocidura beatus), researchers recorded arthropod remains in 100% (Heaney et al., 2006, Table 5). The species was originally described as Crocidura beatus (G. S. Miller, 1910). Its historical type locality is Summit of Mount Bliss, 1461 m, Mindanao, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 uses Crocidura beata, replacing the historical spelling C. beatus through grammatical gender agreement (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A Field Museum Mindanao rapid color guide lists head-and-body length 99 mm, tail length 58 mm and hind-foot length 19 mm for this shrew (Heaney et al., n.d.). The Mount Malindang White-toothed Shrew is historically known from the Mount Malindang region of western Mindanao; broader current occurrence has not been documented in the cited original description (Miller, 1910). The Mount Malindang White-toothed Shrew inhabits montane forest on Mount Malindang, with historical accounts also associating it with primary forest (Wilson & Reeder, 2005). Compiled dietary traits include invertebrates, carrion, and ectothermic vertebrates, with ground foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Crocidura grandis (G. S. Miller, 1910). Its historical type locality is Grand Malindang Mountain, 6100 ft (= 1859 m), Mindanao, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The house shrew has a pointed snout, small eyes, prominent external ears and coarse grey-brown fur, with a long, sparsely haired tail. Its musky odor can be conspicuous at close range (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). For specimens presented in a Mindanao rapid color guide, head-and-body length is 99–131 mm, tail length 54–69 mm and hind-foot length 17–22 mm. These dimensions alone are insufficient for separating every similarly sized shrew (Heaney et al., n.d.). The Asian House Shrew has records from Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kalatungan Range and Bukidnon. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Asian House Shrew is an introduced commensal species found mainly in towns and farmland, sometimes entering disturbed forest. It is predominantly nocturnal and feeds largely on invertebrates (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Sorex murinus (Linnaeus, 1766). Its historical type locality is "Java," Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: Long-tailed macaques have grey-brown to reddish-brown fur, a brownish-grey face, cheek whiskers and a tail longer than the head-body length (Bonadio, n.d.). The Hijo Forest species profile notes a tail longer than the combined head-and-body length, a useful external character of the long-tailed macaque (Gamalo et al., 2023). The Long-tailed Macaque has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Long-tailed Macaque uses forest, woodland, riverine and mangrove habitats, as well as disturbed areas. It lives in social groups, foraging in trees and on the ground for fruit, plant material, insects and other animal foods (Bonadio, n.d.; Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). The species was originally described as Simia fascicularis (Raffles, 1821). Its historical type locality is Indonesia, Sumatra, (Bengkulu) (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Philippine Tarsier has a round face, very large forward-facing eyes and prominent ears. Long hind limbs and slender digits with gripping pads support movement through vegetation, while the long, slender tail bears a tuft toward its tip (University of Michigan Museum of Zoology, n.d.). The Philippine Tarsier has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Magdiwata, Bega Watershed, and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Tarsier uses regenerating secondary lowland forest on Bohol and has been documented sleeping among trees, thickets, screw pines and palms in a mangrove landscape on Siargao (Bejar et al., 2026; Neri-Arboleda, 2002). On Siargao, three tagged adult males had a mean minimum-convex-polygon home range of 3.16 ha (Bejar et al., 2026). At Corella, Bohol, radio-tracking estimated mean home ranges of 6.45 ha for males and 2.45 ha for females (Neri-Arboleda, 2002). A separate captive study examined sex-specific and social-context differences in activity budgets and reported increased travel during the mating season, particularly among males (Wojciechowski et al., 2019). The species was originally described as Simia Syrichta (Linnaeus, 1758). Its historical type locality is "Luzon." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).
