records.p: Compared with Apomys insignis, the Mt. Kitanglad account describes a shorter tail, shorter and broader hind feet, and longer rostrum (Heaney et al., 2006). The Mindanao Mossy Forest Mouse has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo, and Bukidnon (Mearns, 1905; Heaney et al., 2006; American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Records from Mindanao include montane and mossy rainforest, especially at higher elevations on major mountains (Heaney et al., 2006). In a Mount Kitanglad sample of 40 stomachs, arthropods occurred in every specimen and plant material in 95% (Heaney et al., 2006, Table 5). The species was originally described as Apomys hylocœtes (Mearns, 1905). Its historical type locality is "Mount Apo at 6,000 feet altitude [= 1829 m], southern Mindanao, Philippine Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 uses the original spelling Apomys hylocoetes, which also appears in older literature as A. hylocetes (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

Compared with Apomys hylocoetes, this forest mouse has a relatively longer tail, longer narrower hind feet and shorter rostrum in the paired morphological treatment (Heaney et al., 2006). The Mindanao Montane Forest Mouse is recorded on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount McKinley, Mount Lumot, Mount Daguma, and Misamis Oriental. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mindanao Montane Forest Mouse inhabits montane forest. Mount Kitanglad stomach records contain both plant and arthropod material, and compiled traits describe chiefly nocturnal foraging on the ground (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Apomys insignis (Mearns, 1905). Its historical type locality is "Mount Apo at 6,000 feet altitude [= 1829 m], southern Mindanao, Philippine Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

PanTHERIA compiles adult mass 30.9 g and head–body length 109.5 mm for the historical species concept (Jones et al., 2009). The Mindanao Lowland Forest Mouse has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Daguma. On Leyte, records include Mount Pangasugan (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mindanao Lowland Forest Mouse is associated with forests and is described in compiled traits as a nocturnal ground-forager eating plant material and invertebrates (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits include other plant material and invertebrates, with ground foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Rattus (Apomys) littoralis (Sanborn, 1952). Its historical type locality is "Bugasan, altitude 50 feet [= 15 m], Cotabato Province, Mindanao Island, Philippine Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A long, narrow snout and small eyes and ears form part of the published external diagnosis (Rowsey et al., 2022). Dense dark fur covers the body. The visibly haired tail tapers and is shorter than head-and-body length (Rowsey et al., 2022). The type-series comparison reports head-and-body lengths of 131–143 mm and a tail close to 74% of head-and-body length (Rowsey et al., 2022). The published comparison uses external proportions and cranial traits, not snout shape alone, to distinguish Baletemys from related Philippine shrew-mice (Rowsey et al., 2022). The Kampalili Shrew Mouse is documented from montane and mossy forests of Mount Kampalili in eastern Mindanao (Rowsey et al., 2022). The Kampalili Shrew Mouse inhabits old-growth montane and mossy forest on Mount Kampalili, where it has been found under moss-covered fallen logs. Earthworms were used as bait in some original captures but are not confirmed as part of its diet (Rowsey et al., 2022). Baletemys was described as a separate genus in 2022 and is recognized in Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 (Rowsey et al., 2022; American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The mammal database documents a description from lower montane forest of Mount Kampalili in Mindanao (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The species was originally described as Baletemys kampalili (Rowsey, M. R. M. Duya, Ibañez, Jansa, Rickart, & Heaney, 2022). Its historical type locality is lower montane forest of Mount Kampalili, Davao Oriental, Mindanao, at approximately 1,640 m elevation (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: A medium-sized hairy-tailed rat with yellowish-brown, comparatively coarse fur and unusually long whiskers around and above the eyes. Compared with B. salomonseni, the original description notes a shorter relative tail and coarser, shorter pelage; secure distinction also uses skull and tooth characters (Balete et al., 2008). The Hamiguitan Hairy-tailed Rat has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range (GBIF.org, 2026). The Hamiguitan Hairy-tailed Rat inhabits montane forest on Mount Hamiguitan, where it was more frequently captured in primary montane forest than in lower transitional forest during the original study (Balete et al., 2008). The species was originally described as Batomys hamiguitan (Balete, Heaney, Rickart, Quidlat, & Ibanez, 2008). Its historical type locality is Mt. Hamiguitan, Eastern Mindanao Island, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The original description distinguished Batomys hamiguitan from B. salomonseni using a combination of cranial and dental characters (Balete et al., 2008).

A relatively small hairy-tailed rat with conspicuously russet-colored fur, unlike the larger, more somber-brown congeners compared in its original description. Detailed confirmation uses additional cranial and vascular characters; color and size alone should not substitute for specialist assessment (Musser et al., 1998). The Russet Hairy-tailed Rat is documented on Dinagat Island in the Greater Mindanao PAIC. The cited original description does not establish its occurrence on mainland Mindanao (Musser et al., 1998). The Russet Hairy-tailed Rat inhabits lowland evergreen rainforest on Dinagat. Compiled traits describe mainly nocturnal ground-foraging on plant material, fruit and seeds (Musser et al., 1998; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Batomys russatus (Musser, Heaney, & Tabaranza, 1998). Its historical type locality is Libjo (= Albor), Plaridel Municipality, Surigao del Norte Province, Dinagat Island, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: PanTHERIA compiles adult mass 185.8 g and head–body length 175.0 mm for the historical species concept (Jones et al., 2009). The Mindanao Hairy-tailed Rat is recorded on Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kalatungan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Lumot, and Misamis Oriental. On Leyte, records include Mount Pangasugan and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Mindanao Hairy-tailed Rat inhabits montane and mossy forests, including Mount Kitanglad. Stomach observations include plant material, and compiled traits describe nocturnal ground-foraging (Heaney et al., 2006; Balete et al., 2008; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Mindanaomys salomonseni (Sanborn, 1953). Its historical type locality is Mt. Katanglad, Bukidnon Province, Mindanao Island, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A trapped individual from eastern Samar was distinguished from Rattus everetti by the tail being noticeably shorter than head-and-body length, together with relatively long, moderately broad hind feet (Fernandez et al., 2020). The Mindanao Forest Rat has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Mindanao Forest Rat is associated with forests. Plant remains and small amounts of arthropod material were found in stomach samples from Mount Kitanglad; the compiled traits describe primarily ground-based, nocturnal foraging (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). All three examined Mt Kitanglad stomachs contained plant remains (Heaney et al., 2006). In three stomachs examined from Mt. Kitanglad, researchers recorded trace arthropod remains in all 3 specimens (Heaney et al., 2006, Table 5). EltonTraits summarizes the diet as other plant material (60%), seeds (20%), fruit (10%), invertebrates (10%), with ground foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Bullimus bagobus (Mearns, 1905). Its historical type locality is "Todaya, a Bagobo village at 4,000 feet [= 1219 m] altitude on Mount Apo, southern Mindanao [Island], Philippine Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Dinagat Bushy-tailed Cloud Rat is a large, long-furred rodent with orangish-tawny upperparts mixed with black guard hairs and a paler orangish-brown underside. Its conspicuously hairy tail is tawny near the base, black through most of its length, and white at the tip. The published descriptive treatment places it between the larger Luzon C. schadenbergi and the smaller Ilin C. paulus in body size (Plazi TreatmentBank, n.d.). The Dinagat Bushy-tailed Cloud Rat is recorded from Dinagat Island, particularly the forest landscapes of Dinagat Islands Province (Pitogo et al., 2026). The Dinagat Bushy-tailed Cloud Rat is associated with forest and has compiled traits of nocturnal tree-foraging on fruit and other plant material (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits include fruit and other plant material, with arboreal foraging and nocturnal and crepuscular activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The Philippine Department of Environment and Natural Resources identifies Dinagat hairy-tailed cloud rat Crateromys australis as Critically Endangered in its national threatened-species discussion (Department of Environment and Natural Resources, n.d.). The species was originally described as Crateromys australis (Musser, Heaney, & Rabor, 1985). Its historical type locality is "Balitbiton, Loreto Municipality, Dinagat Island, Surigao del Norte Province, Republic of the Philippines." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

records.p: A small, dark-furred shrew-mouse with short ears, small eyes and a comparatively short tail. Its dorsal coat has stiff, spiny hairs rather than the softer pelage of the sympatric Katanglad Shrew Mouse, C. suncoides. This coat-texture comparison is supported by the genus-level reappraisal of Giarla and colleagues (2025); external characters alone do not constitute a full specimen diagnosis. The Mindanao Shrew Mouse is recorded on Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Matutum, and Mount Daguma. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Mindanao Shrew Mouse is associated with montane habitats. In the Mount Kitanglad sample, stomachs contained both plants and arthropods; a wider trait compilation describes ground-based, mainly diurnal foraging (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). Small stomach samples contained both plant and arthropod remains (Heaney et al., 2006). Compiled traits describe a largely plant-based diet, ground foraging and daytime activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Crunomys melanius (O. Thomas, 1907). Its historical type locality is "North Central Mindanao [Island, Philippines]. 3000' [= 914 m]." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Katanglad Shrew Mouse belongs to a group of dark-coated murid rodents with small eyes and ears and a short tail. Its coat is soft rather than spiny, in contrast to the Mindanao Shrew Mouse, C. melanius (Giarla et al., 2025). The comparison is based on taxonomic descriptions, and the species was originally described from limited specimen material. The Katanglad Shrew Mouse has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kalatungan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Lumot, Misamis Oriental, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Katanglad Shrew Mouse has been recorded in upper montane rainforest on Mount Kitanglad. One examined stomach contained arthropod remains; compiled traits also describe plant material in its diet (Rickart et al., 1998; Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Crunomys suncoides (Rickart, Heaney, Tabaranza, & Balete, 1998). Its historical type locality is "Mt. Katanglad Range, 18.5 km S, 4 km E Camp Phillips, Bukidnon Province, Mindanao Island, Philippines, 2250 m elevation, 8°9'30"N, 124°51'E." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: Relative to L. sibuanus, this mouse has longer hind feet and tail, softer fur and greyish-white underparts (Rickart et al., 2003). Distinguished from L. sibuanus by softer coat and a longer tail (Rickart et al., 2003). The Gray-bellied Moss Mouse has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kalatungan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Gray-bellied Moss Mouse inhabits upland forest on Mount Kitanglad, where it moves on the ground and through vegetation. Its diet includes plant material, and it is mainly active at night (Rickart et al., 2003; Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Limnomys bryophilus (Rickart, Heaney, & Tabaranza, 2003). Its historical type locality is 18.5 km S, 4 km E Camp Phillips, 2250 m, Mount Kitanglad Range, Bukidnon Province, north-central Mindanao Island, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: Compared with the closely related L. bryophilus, its hind feet and tail are shorter and the underparts paler (Rickart et al., 2003). The shorter hind feet and shorter tail help separate it from L. bryophilus (Rickart et al., 2003). The Long-tailed Moss Mouse has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kalatungan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Matutum, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Long-tailed Moss Mouse is associated with forests. Plant material occurred in the Mount Kitanglad stomach samples, and compiled traits describe nocturnal foraging both on the ground and in vegetation (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). Stomach samples from Mount Kitanglad contained plant material (Heaney et al., 2006). Compiled traits indicate mainly plant-based feeding, some climbing while foraging, and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Limnomys sibuanus (Mearns, 1905). Its historical type locality is Mount Apo, 2012 m, Davao City Province, south-eastern Mindanao, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

PanTHERIA compiles adult mass 19.3 g for the historical species concept (Jones et al., 2009). The House Mouse has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Daguma and Sultan Kudarat (GBIF.org, 2026). The House Mouse commonly occupies settlements and other disturbed habitats and forages mainly at night on seeds, other plant material and invertebrates (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled traits describe ground foraging, largely nocturnal activity, and a diet of seeds, other plant material and invertebrates (Wilman et al., 2014). Comparative reproductive data report litters with multiple young (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Mus Musculus (Linnaeus, 1758). Its historical type locality is Uppsala, Sweden (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Hijo study describes the Philippine forest rat as having a dark basal tail and a contrasting white distal portion that can occupy roughly 20–50% of the tail length. The field-guide caution that tail coloration alone may not resolve all murid identifications still applies (Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Forest Rat has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Forest Rat inhabits forest and forages mainly on the ground at night. Its diet includes seeds, fruit, other plant material and invertebrates (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Mus everetti (A. Günther, 1879). Its historical type locality is northern Mindanao Island, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).
